paragraphs.heading: The maths of waiting in line
paragraphs.text: Queueing theory is the mathematical study of queues, which are simply waiting lines. Its models are built so that you can predict how long a queue will get and how long people will wait in it. It is usually counted as a branch of operations research. That is because its results often feed business decisions about how many resources a service needs.

paragraphs.heading: Born in a telephone exchange
paragraphs.text: The field began with Agner Krarup Erlang, who built models of the calls coming in to the Copenhagen Telephone Exchange Company. His ideas laid the ground for teletraffic engineering. They have since spread to telecommunications, traffic engineering, computing and project management. They are used most of all in industrial engineering, to design factories, shops, offices and hospitals.

paragraphs.heading: Answers in odds, not certainties
paragraphs.text: Queueing analysis deals in probability, so its results, called operating characteristics, are likely values rather than fixed ones. The aim is to work these out for the system as it stands, then try several alternatives that might do better. Setting the numbers side by side shows managers the pros and cons of each option. That helps them find ways to save money, cut waiting time and run more efficiently.

paragraphs.heading: A supermarket checkout
paragraphs.text: In the theory, jobs arrive at a queue, perhaps wait, spend some time being served, and then leave. Jobs may be called customers or requests depending on the field. A queue has one or more servers, and each server is paired with an arriving job and becomes free again once that job is done and departs. A supermarket cashier is the usual picture: one cashier serving one shopper at a time is a queue with a single server. If shoppers walk away whenever the cashier is busy, the queue has no buffer, while room for up to n waiting shoppers is a buffer of size n.

paragraphs.heading: A shorthand for queues
paragraphs.text: A single queue is usually labelled in Kendall's notation, A/S/c. A says how the times between arrivals are spread out, S says how service times are spread out, and c is the number of servers. The M/M/1 queue is a simple case: one server, jobs arriving as a Poisson process, and service times that are exponentially distributed, with M standing for a Markov process. In an M/G/1 queue the G means service times can follow any distribution. David George Kendall introduced this notation in 1953.

paragraphs.heading: From formulas to the Internet
paragraphs.text: Felix Pollaczek solved the M/G/1 queue in 1930, and Aleksandr Khinchin later restated the answer in terms of probability, giving the Pollaczek–Khinchine formula. John Kingman found a formula for the average wait in a G/G/1 queue. In the early 1960s Leonard Kleinrock applied queueing theory to message switching, and in the early 1970s to packet switching. The theory he published in the early 1970s underpinned packet switching in the ARPANET, a forerunner of the Internet.
